title: Intermediate Marathon Training Plan (18 Weeks)
excerpt: Every week of an intermediate marathon schedule in miles and km, for runners with a marathon done and 30-35 mi (48-56 km) a week. Peaks at 55 mi (89 km).
body:
Intermediate Marathon Training Plan (18 Weeks)

This intermediate marathon training plan is for runners who have finished at least one marathon, currently run 30–35 miles (48–56 km) a week, and want to run faster. It runs for 18 weeks on five or six days a week, peaking at 55 miles (89 km). Long runs reach 22 miles (35 km), and several of them finish at goal marathon pace. Every week is listed below in miles and kilometres, with a pace key and guidance on adjusting the plan.

Not sure which plan? Compare them here.

Who this plan is for

  • You have run at least one marathon and want to improve your time.
  • You currently run 5 days a week, totalling 30–35 miles (48–56 km), with a long run of 12+ miles (19 km).
  • You can handle two quality sessions a week: one workout and one marathon-pace (MP) run or MP finish.
  • Your race is 18 weeks away.

Running less than 30 miles a week? The 16 week plan peaks at 48. If you already run 40+ miles a week and want more volume, look at the higher tiers described in our guide to Pfitzinger's marathon plans.

What makes this plan "intermediate"

Compared with a first-marathon plan, three things change:

  • More volume: a mid-week aerobic run of 7–11 miles (11–18 km) on Wednesdays builds endurance without another long run.
  • Specific long runs: four long runs finish with 3–6 miles (5–10 km) at MP, so you practise holding race pace on tired legs.
  • A sixth day: a short easy run on Friday from week 5, which you can drop if you need to.

The full 18-week schedule (miles & km)

Tuesday alternates between threshold (T) and interval (I) sessions. Wednesday is the mid-week aerobic run. Saturday has either strides or an MP run. Sunday is the long run. Monday is a rest day, and so is Friday in weeks 1–4 and in cutback and taper weeks.

Pace key

  • Easy: conversational, about 60–90 s/mi (35–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace.
  • Long run: easy pace, 45–90 s/mi (30–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace, except segments marked @ MP.
  • MP: your goal marathon pace.
  • T (threshold): comfortably hard, the pace you could race for about an hour. Roughly 25–40 s/mi (15–25 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 2 min between reps.
  • I (intervals): 5K–10K effort, roughly 50–80 s/mi (30–50 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 90 s–2 min between reps.
  • Hills: 60 s uphill at 5K effort; jog back down.
  • Strides: 20 s quick and relaxed at the end of an easy run. Walk back to recover.
  • Workout distances include a 1–2 mi (2–3 km) warm-up and cool-down.

How the 18 weeks are built

  • Weeks 1–4: volume rises from 34 to 40 miles (55 to 64 km) on five days, then a cutback.
  • Weeks 5–8: the sixth day is added and volume reaches 49 miles (79 km). The first MP finish comes in week 7.
  • Weeks 9–12: long runs reach 20 miles (32 km), and the week-11 long run includes 6 miles (10 km) at MP.
  • Weeks 13–15: peak volume of 53–55 miles (85–89 km). The 22-mile (35 km) long run in week 15 finishes with 6 miles at MP, three weeks before the race.
  • Weeks 16–18: taper, at 43, 34 and 18 miles (69, 55 and 29 km).

How to adjust the plan

  • Five days only: drop the Friday run. The peak becomes about 51 miles (82 km).
  • Only 16 weeks available: start at week 3, provided you are already running 38–40 miles a week.
  • The 22-miler: if it would take you more than about 3 hours 15 minutes, cap it at 3:15 and keep the MP finish.
  • Goal pace: base MP on a recent half marathon (about 2.1 × your half time) or your last marathon, whichever is more recent. Don't base it on a hoped-for time.
  • Kilometres: follow the km values. They are rounded.
  • Pain or injury: pain that changes how you run, or doesn't ease within a few days, means stop and see a doctor or physio. Don't run through it.

Fueling, strength and race week

MP long runs are the time to rehearse race fueling at race intensity. Aim for the carbohydrate intake you plan to use on race day. Keep strength work heavy and short, twice a week, until week 15. Our guide to what a marathon plan should include covers fueling and strength in depth.

Related plans

  • Sub 4 hour marathon training plan: if your goal is specifically to break four hours.
  • 16 week marathon training plan: lower volume, peaking at 48 miles.
  • Pfitzinger marathon training plans explained: higher-mileage plans for experienced marathoners.

FAQ

What counts as an intermediate marathon runner?

Generally, someone who has finished at least one marathon, runs consistently 4–6 days a week, and is comfortable with structured workouts. Your finish time doesn't decide it. Your training history does.

How many miles a week should an intermediate marathoner run?

Peaks of 45–60 miles (72–97 km) are typical. This plan peaks at 55 miles (89 km), and every non-cutback week from week 9 onward falls between 52 and 55 miles (84–89 km).

Should intermediate runners run longer than 20 miles?

One run of 21–22 miles is reasonable if it takes no more than about 3:15. Beyond that, extra distance adds more fatigue than fitness.

Is 18 weeks too long for an intermediate plan?

Not if you are starting at 30–35 miles a week. The first four weeks get you to the volume that the specific work needs. If you are already at 40+ miles, you can start at week 3.
keyTakeaway: Going faster after your first marathon comes from more easy volume, a mid-week aerobic run and long runs that finish at marathon pace, not from more speed work.
